verification.passage_check: Independently reconciled all 45 pages of the exact SHA-pinned arXiv v6 PDF and extraction, including Equations 1-20, Table 1, Figures 1-6, Tables S1-S3, Figures S1-S12, the complete supplement, and the immutable PyDaDDy v1.1.1 artifact. The second pass confirmed the printed Equation 6 and Equation 7 inconsistencies, synthetic and biological result boundaries, held-out split, limited-data failures, multidimensional implementation defects, generic-versus-manual residual paths, and artifact timebase metadata contradictions.
verification.competitor_check: Independently checked the official primary records and exact current versions for the full competitor panel through 2026-08-24, adding HyperSINDy v1 as a material stochastic-equation successor and the official UAI 2026 PMLR sparse-drift paper as an adjacent current method for repeated short trajectories.

question: Can local Kramers-Moyal estimates plus sparse regression recover compact Ito drift and diffusion equations from uniformly sampled biological time series, and do PyDaDDy's diagnostics make those equations trustworthy on synthetic, fish-schooling, and confined-cell data?

key_findings.claim: The defensible method is a convenient synthesis of established jump-moment estimation and stochastic SINDy, not a new identification principle.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 1-6 estimate an Ito drift f and diffusion tensor G=gg^T from one-step increments, then fit each component independently with sequentially thresholded least squares over a user-supplied library. Boninsegna et al. had already extended SINDy to stochastic drift and diffusion in 2017-2018, while Langevin regression and Stochastic Force Inference already supplied finite-time, high-dimensional, and statistical-consistency machinery. The paper's real contribution is the end-to-end PyDaDDy interface, visualization, examples, and diagnostic workflow.

key_findings.claim: The four headline synthetic examples recover their in-library polynomial equations closely, but they are favorable specification checks rather than broad discovery evidence.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 reports drift estimates -0.995x, 0.902x-0.967x^3, 1.924x-2.879x^3, and -0.992x, and diffusion estimates close to the four generating functions. These selected systems use the same polynomial representation that the regression searches, report no independent test trajectories, seed repetitions, false-selection rates, or out-of-library cases, and show samples rather than a comparative benchmark. Thus the panels demonstrate coefficient recovery under correct library specification, not general equation identifiability.

key_findings.claim: The classic ecology table expands coverage, but it relies on large simulated datasets and libraries containing the ground-truth functional responses.
key_findings.evidence: Supplement S3 simulates 10^6 Euler-Maruyama points at delta t=0.01 for logistic, harvesting, lake eutrophication, Lotka-Volterra competition, Van der Pol, and predator-prey systems. Nonpolynomial cases receive hand-built libraries containing the relevant rational response term; harvesting and competition pool multiple initial conditions for state-space coverage. Table 1 coefficients are generally close, but the harvesting fit includes a -4.61 constant and the evaluation gives neither standardized structure-selection accuracy nor uncertainty across repeated discovery runs.

anchors.section: Supplement S3 / simulation and library details

key_findings.claim: The fish equation reproduces a previously reported noise-induced-schooling result; its strongest new value here is workflow reproduction, not mechanism discovery.
key_findings.evidence: Using about 24,635 packaged polarization samples at 0.12 s spacing, the paper fits m-dot=-0.16m+sqrt(0.26(1-|m|^2)) eta and interprets the mode near |m|=1 despite deterministic equilibrium m=0 as noise-induced order. The text explicitly says Jhawar et al. 2020 had already inferred this mechanism by conventional jump moments and that this study tests whether PyDaDDy recovers it. Histogram agreement is good, but the model misses the negative approximately 10 s autocorrelation attributed to tank-boundary motion.

key_findings.claim: The confined-cell model is descriptively useful but fails the paper's own Gaussian-noise assumption and is partly selected using the statistics later called diagnostics.
key_findings.evidence: The paper rejects an overdamped position-only SDE because residual and model autocorrelations fail, then fits an underdamped x-dot=v model with cubic drift and quartic diffusion. Figure 6A visibly shows a residual distribution more centrally concentrated than the standard Gaussian; the text concedes this while still claiming broad histogram/autorrelation agreement. Supplement S4 says the quartic diffusion was chosen because lower-order noise models failed to reproduce the x histogram and physical boundaries. Long-run histograms and autocorrelations therefore were not in the sparse-regression loss, but they were used iteratively for model selection and are not untouched confirmatory tests.

key_findings.claim: The left-out comparisons support transfer of coarse summary statistics, not predictive validation of transition dynamics or exact equation structure.
key_findings.evidence: The paper trains on two of four fish trials and 75 of 149 cell trajectories, then compares model-generated versus held-out histograms and autocorrelations. Figure S8 shows close histograms and broad autocorrelation agreement, although the fish anticorrelation mismatch remains. No held-out one-step likelihood, transition density, pathwise forecast, coefficient stability, calibration, or alternative-model comparison is reported. Many different stochastic processes can share these two summaries, so the evidence supports limited distributional generalization only.

key_findings.claim: The limited-data study correctly exposes dependence on record length, sampling interval, and state-space coverage, while weakening rhetoric that sparse regression eliminates sampling choices.
key_findings.evidence: A 1,000-point delta t=0.01 record confined to one region and a coarsely sampled 1 s record yield incorrect equations, large coefficient uncertainties, and autocorrelation failures in Figure S11. Figures S9-S10 average 100 synthetic realizations and show drift error falling with length and both drift and diffusion error increasing as sampling gets coarser. The package avoids choosing an extra subsampling lag for its preferred estimator, but it still requires uniformly sampled, sufficiently fine raw data and a suitable analysis timescale, so temporal-resolution dependence is not eliminated.

key_findings.claim: The printed diffusion and residual equations are internally inconsistent with standard Ito scaling and with the archived implementation.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 5 defines epsilon(t)=x(t+delta t)-x(t)-delta t fhat(x(t)), already a one-step residual increment, but Equation 6 estimates G from [epsilon(t+delta t)-epsilon(t)] squared over delta t rather than epsilon(t)epsilon(t)^T/delta t. Equation 7 then standardizes the instantaneous velocity residual only by sqrt(G), omitting the necessary sqrt(delta t) factor. The archived scalar sparse-fit path instead computes epsilon squared over delta t. The generic analysis.py diagnostic path divides the increment residual by sqrt(delta t) but does not divide by state-dependent sqrt(G), whereas cell notebook 8 manually computes (drift_raw-F2)/sqrt(G22), matching the printed Equation 7 operation after its sampling step is nondimensionalized to one. The manuscript diffusion formula, estimator, generic diagnostic, and manual cell diagnostic are therefore distinct operations; the omitted state-dependent normalization does not describe every published diagnostic path.

key_findings.claim: The exact archived PyDaDDy v1.1.1 artifact contains implementation defects that directly affect multidimensional diffusion and noise diagnostics.
key_findings.evidence: In Zenodo record 13777396, commit snapshot 0db76ee, sde.py computes y diffusion by calling _diffusion_y_from_residual with F1 rather than F2. Its cross-diffusion residual subtracts drift without multiplying by the sampling interval and scales the product as t_int/dt rather than by 1/(t_int dt). The generic analysis.py path comments out division by the fitted diffusion in both scalar and vector residual diagnostics, although cell notebook 8 separately performs manual state-dependent normalization. Simulation takes sqrt(abs(G)) for scalar and diagonal vector cases, silently reflecting negative fitted diffusion instead of enforcing a nonnegative scalar or positive-semidefinite tensor. These are source-level findings; the paper's reported coefficients were not independently rerun.

key_findings.claim: The public artifact is substantial but does not provide a clean, tested paper-reproduction path.
key_findings.evidence: The immutable Zenodo archive has the claimed MD5, GPL-3 source, six packaged datasets, nine tutorial notebooks, and explicit fish and cell workflows. However, it has no CI configuration, only four simulation-oriented unit tests, no inference-correctness regression tests, no environment lock, and unpinned lower-bound dependencies. The paper's cell notebook silently mirrors all 149 trajectories by stacking x and -x, a preprocessing choice absent from the manuscript, and selects manual thresholds. Artifact timebase metadata are also contradictory: the paper and archived loader use 0.12 s for fish and 1/6 h=10 min for cell velocity construction, while the archived README states 0.04 s and 15 min, respectively; this audit does not choose one source as authoritative. PyPI currently exposes only versions 1.0.0 and 0.1.5 despite the archive and setup.py declaring 1.1.1. A local test collection failed because plotly was not installed in the audit environment; no paper-result reproduction was attempted.

method.core_idea: Estimate local Ito drift and covariance from finite increments, fit sparse analytic functions to the unbinned pointwise estimates, and use residual, simulation, self-consistency, and held-out-data checks to decide whether the resulting SDE is an adequate low-dimensional description.
method.mechanism: Given a uniformly sampled scalar or two-component series, PyDaDDy forms one-step drift targets and drift-corrected squared residuals for diffusion. STLSQ repeatedly solves ridge or least-squares regressions over polynomial or custom libraries and removes coefficients below a threshold. The threshold can be chosen from five-fold contiguous KFold error by taking the largest jump in error, or set manually. The fitted SDE is simulated to compare histograms and autocorrelations and is re-estimated for self-consistency; residual shape, correlation, QQ plots, and a scalar Pawula check probe assumptions.
assumptions: The observed state is a continuous-path, stationary, Markov Ito diffusion at the chosen temporal resolution.
The driving innovations are temporally white and Gaussian after conditioning on the observed state.
The observed variables form a sufficiently complete low-dimensional state; omitted slow variables do not leave memory in residuals.
The raw sampling interval is much shorter than the state autocorrelation time and finite-delta bias is acceptably small.
Available trajectories cover enough of state space to identify global rather than merely local dynamics.
Drift and diffusion lie in, or are well approximated by, the candidate library and its columns are sufficiently distinguishable over sampled states.
STLSQ coefficient magnitude is meaningful after variable scaling and threshold choice.
Five contiguous folds provide a useful model-selection score despite dependence between adjacent time samples.
For multidimensional data, only G=gg^T is identifiable; a particular matrix square root g is not unique.
Independently fitted diffusion components form a nonnegative scalar or positive-semidefinite tensor throughout every state visited in simulation.
Sporadic NaNs propagate through finite differences and are removed without converting a physical gap into a one-step transition.
Measurement error is small enough that its known upward bias on diffusion does not dominate process noise.
Histogram and autocorrelation agreement are adequate descriptive criteria even though they do not identify a unique transition law.

techniques.role: Forms finite-sampling estimates of conditional drift and covariance from observed increments.
Subtracts estimated deterministic increments before fitting diffusion to reduce finite-time drift contamination.
Iteratively removes small library coefficients to obtain an interpretable sparse equation.
Allows biologically motivated polynomial, rational, Fourier, or other candidate functions.
Chooses a sparsity threshold from the maximum increase in contiguous five-fold validation error.
Examines residual distributions, QQ plots, and temporal autocorrelation against white-Gaussian assumptions.
Compares scalar second and fourth Kramers-Moyal moments as an advanced diffusion diagnostic.
Compares simulated and observed histograms and autocorrelation functions.
Re-runs discovery on simulated model output to test estimator closure.
Fits selected trials or trajectories and checks coarse statistics against the remaining data.
Nondimensionalizes position and velocity so coefficient magnitude thresholding is meaningful.
Combines initial conditions or replicate trajectories to improve state-space coverage.

evaluations.setting: Four scalar synthetic Ito SDEs with nearly paired unimodal or bimodal stationary histograms
evaluations.metric: Recovered symbolic structure and displayed coefficient estimates
evaluations.result: Figure 2 recovers the correct active polynomial terms and coefficients close to ground truth for all four in-library examples
evaluations.baseline: The generating drift and diffusion functions

evaluations.setting: Six stochastic ecology and oscillator models simulated for 10^6 points at delta t=0.01
evaluations.metric: Qualitative structural and coefficient agreement in Table 1
evaluations.result: Most terms and coefficients are close, although some spurious or shifted terms remain and nonpolynomial cases use ground-truth-informed libraries
evaluations.baseline: Logistic, harvesting, eutrophication, competition, Van der Pol, and predator-prey generating equations

evaluations.setting: Record lengths 10^4 to 10^6 across four scalar synthetic SDEs, 100 realizations each
evaluations.metric: Relative RMSE of drift and diffusion functions
evaluations.result: Sparse fits generally beat binwise averages; drift improves with record length while diffusion error changes less systematically
evaluations.baseline: Conventional binwise Kramers-Moyal averaging and manual versus automatic thresholds

evaluations.setting: Increasing sampling intervals for the same four synthetic systems
evaluations.metric: Relative RMSE of drift and diffusion
evaluations.result: PyDaDDy error increases with coarser sampling; binwise estimates sometimes have a bias-variance minimum at an intermediate lag
evaluations.baseline: Binwise estimates and manual threshold fits

evaluations.setting: Karimeen fish-school polarization, about one hour and 24,635 packaged two-dimensional samples
evaluations.metric: Residual shape/correlation, histogram, autocorrelation, and self-consistency
evaluations.result: The fitted linear-drift quadratic-diffusion SDE reproduces the noise-induced-order interpretation and |m| histogram but misses the negative approximately 10 s autocorrelation
evaluations.baseline: Observed data and Jhawar et al. 2020's prior jump-moment result

evaluations.setting: 149 confined-cell migration trajectories sampled every 10 minutes for up to 50 hours
evaluations.metric: Residual diagnostics and simulated position/velocity histogram and autocorrelation
evaluations.result: An overdamped model fails; a cubic-drift quartic-diffusion underdamped model broadly matches coarse statistics, but residuals are distinctly non-Gaussian
evaluations.baseline: Overdamped SDE, constant diffusion, quadratic diffusion, and Brückner et al. 2019's binwise limit-cycle model

evaluations.setting: Held-out two-of-four fish trials and 74-of-149 cell trajectories
evaluations.result: Figure S8 reports good coarse-statistic agreement, without likelihood, transition, coefficient-stability, or pathwise predictive metrics

evaluations.setting: Fish package workload with about 25,000 two-dimensional points
evaluations.result: Paper reports about 800 ms for coefficient estimation, 2 ms for drift fit, and 6 ms for diffusion fit on a 2023 M2 Mac Mini; Colab times are 2.5 s, 10 ms, and 60 ms
evaluations.baseline: No competing implementation or repeated timing distribution

limitations: Only one- and two-dimensional visualization and diagnostics are implemented, while polynomial libraries grow combinatorially in higher dimensions.
The procedure assumes a Markov Ito diffusion with continuous paths and white Gaussian innovations; jumps, colored noise, non-Gaussian forcing, and time-varying parameters are outside scope.
The cell residual visibly violates the Gaussian assumption, so that real-data equation is at best a descriptive effective model.

Equation 6 and Equation 7 have scaling/form inconsistencies; generic archived diagnostics do not implement the printed standardized residual, while the manual cell notebook separately uses the Equation 7 form after nondimensionalizing its sampling step to one.
The archived multidimensional code uses the x-drift F1 when estimating y diffusion and mis-scales cross diffusion.
Independent component fits do not guarantee a positive-semidefinite diffusion tensor; simulation sometimes applies absolute values instead of enforcing admissibility.
Finite sampling introduces bias, and the paper offers no finite-delta correction comparable to adjoint Fokker-Planck Langevin regression.
Measurement noise is not modeled separately and is expected to bias diffusion by the measurement-noise variance.
Short records, coarse sampling, incomplete state-space coverage, omitted variables, and correlated library columns can all produce wrong equations.
Coefficient-magnitude thresholding depends on variable scaling, and the cell analysis requires hand nondimensionalization.
The maximum-CV-error-jump threshold is heuristic; temporal folds are dependent, and real-data models are selected manually through repeated diagnostic inspection.
Histograms, autocorrelations, and self-consistency are non-identifying checks and do not establish the true transition law.
The fish and cell mechanisms largely reproduce Jhawar et al. 2020 and Brückner et al. 2019 rather than supply independent discoveries.
The package notebook mirrors the cell trajectories without disclosing that preprocessing in the manuscript.
Artifact timebase metadata conflict without a documented reconciliation: the paper and loader use fish 0.12 s and cell 10 min, whereas the archived README states 0.04 s and 15 min.
The reported coefficient error bars are not accompanied by a clear repeated-sample or bootstrap procedure.
No direct accuracy, robustness, or runtime comparison is made against stochastic SINDy, Stochastic Force Inference, Langevin regression, or later PASTIS and weak-form methods.
Current installation metadata are inconsistent: the archived code declares v1.1.1, while PyPI exposes 1.0.0 and 0.1.5.
failure_modes: A short trajectory trapped near one stable state yields a locally plausible but globally wrong phase portrait.
A coarse raw sampling interval destroys fine transition information and biases both drift and diffusion.
Unobserved state variables leave colored or non-Gaussian residuals even if a sparse equation can still be fit.
A candidate library missing the true function forces a spurious combination, while highly correlated basis functions make individual coefficients non-identifiable.
Five-fold threshold tuning can exploit dependence between adjacent samples and favor an unstable support.
Manual iteration against histogram and autocorrelation can overfit the same summaries later presented as validation.
A fitted scalar diffusion can become negative or a tensor indefinite outside the dense data region; applying abs or a generic matrix square root changes the learned model.
The fish diffusion beta(1-|m|^2) becomes negative outside the physical unit disk unless the state domain or boundary is enforced.
The cell quartic diffusion can encode the boundary empirically while confounding measurement, physical constraints, and stochastic forcing.
Measurement error inflates diffusion and can create apparent multiplicative noise.
Changing parameters or nonstationarity can be misrepresented as state-dependent drift or diffusion.
The archived y-diffusion bug contaminates two-dimensional estimates whenever F1 and F2 differ.

The generic archived residual diagnostics can label a heteroskedastic process Gaussian because they omit normalization by fitted state-dependent diffusion; the manual cell notebook uses a distinct normalized path.
Cross-diffusion simulation can fail or become complex when the independently fitted covariance is not positive semidefinite.
Joining heterogeneous trials without explicit boundary NaNs can create artificial transitions at concatenation points.
reusable_insights: Treat drift and diffusion discovery as conditional-transition inference; stationary histograms alone cannot distinguish deterministic and noise-induced states.
Always pair equation discovery with residual whiteness, distributional, finite-time, and held-out transition checks, but keep model-selection diagnostics separate from final validation.
Use multiple initial conditions or interventions to cover state space when the natural process remains near one attractor.
State that multidimensional data identify the covariance G, not a unique noise factor g, and enforce positive semidefiniteness explicitly.
Scale variables before magnitude-based sparsification and report the transformation so coefficients remain interpretable and reproducible.
Compare sparse global fits with local binwise estimates: disagreement can reveal library misspecification or poorly sampled regions.
Audit published equations against implementation, especially powers of delta t in SDE residuals and diffusion estimators.
Use block-aware splits across independent trials or trajectories rather than adjacent samples for honest time-series validation.
Report support stability over resamples, not only OLS-style coefficient error bars after a selected sparse model.
Separate observation noise, process noise, and boundary effects before giving mechanistic meaning to a fitted diffusion function.
An accessible package and diagnostics can be a meaningful systems contribution even when the estimator components are prior art, provided novelty is framed accordingly.
open_questions: What corrections to Equations 6-7 did the authors intend, and which exact code path generated every published residual and diffusion figure?
How do the reported fish and cell equations change after fixing F2 use, cross-diffusion scaling, and state-dependent residual normalization in the archived package?
Can scalar nonnegativity and tensor positive semidefiniteness be imposed during sparse fitting without sacrificing interpretability?
How stable are selected supports and coefficients under trajectory-level bootstrap, alternative folds, and reasonable variable scalings?
Do the real-data models improve held-out transition likelihood, first-passage times, dwell-time distributions, or forecasts over simpler baselines?
Can observation noise and latent colored dynamics be separated from state-dependent process diffusion in these datasets?
How sensitive is the cell quartic diffusion to the undisclosed mirror augmentation and manual threshold choices?
Can symmetry-aware libraries recover the fish vector law directly while preserving the unit-disk boundary?
How does corrected PyDaDDy compare under common data budgets with PASTIS, stochastic SINDy, Langevin regression, Stochastic Force Inference, and weak-form generator discovery?
Can an end-to-end workflow retain PyDaDDy's usability while adding finite-time correction, jump-process alternatives, nonstationarity tests, and trial-level validation?

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse learning of stochastic dynamic equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Boninsegna, Nuske, and Clementi introduced stochastic SINDy before PyDaDDy, proved infinite-data asymptotic correctness for drift and diffusion in original and projected variables, and emphasized cross-validation for sparsity. PyDaDDy's defensible advance is packaging, visualization, biological examples, and diagnostics rather than the sparse stochastic estimator itself.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning force fields from stochastic trajectories
competitive_landscape.difference: Stochastic Force Inference estimates force and spatially varying diffusion efficiently in high dimensions, supplies self-consistent inference errors, information bounds, and robustness to experimental noise. It is less turnkey for ecological users but substantially stronger on statistical efficiency, uncertainty, and high-dimensional scope.

competitive_landscape.title: Nonlinear stochastic modeling with Langevin regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Langevin regression combines sparse model selection with forward and adjoint Fokker-Planck equations, correcting finite-time sampling and enforcing steady-state statistical consistency, including colored or unresolved forcing after subsampling. PyDaDDy is simpler and faster but lacks those finite-time corrections and stronger statistical constraints.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse inference and active learning of stochastic differential equations from data
competitive_landscape.difference: Huang et al. use automatic-threshold sparse Bayesian learning with Laplacian priors, estimate uncertainty, and add feedback interventions to improve rare-state coverage. It directly addresses PyDaDDy's state-space-coverage failure mode but is less focused on an end-user diagnostic package.

competitive_landscape.title: Principled model selection for stochastic dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: PASTIS replaces heuristic threshold selection with likelihood statistics and extreme-value control for combinatorial model search, reporting reliable minimal-model identification under low sampling rates and measurement error and extending to stochastic PDEs and ecological networks. It directly targets PyDaDDy's weakest statistical component: heuristic, dependent-fold support selection.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Stochastic Dynamical Systems with Structured Noise
competitive_landscape.difference: Guo, Greene, and Zhong learn drift and diffusion nonparametrically when the noise covariance is singular, including second-order physical systems and a high-dimensional Cucker-Smale flock reduced by symmetry. This is especially relevant to PyDaDDy's underdamped cell and collective-motion cases, where covariance structure and dimension reduction are handled heuristically.

competitive_landscape.title: Data-Driven Weak-form Discovery of Stochastic Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: This spatial weak-form method averages across trajectories before sparse regression and adds drift-informed diffusion bias correction, reporting coefficient, stationary-density, escape-rate, and finite-sampling results. It directly addresses the pointwise variance and diffusion-bias problems that PyDaDDy treats through raw jump targets and heuristic diagnostics.

competitive_landscape.title: HyperSINDy: Deep Generative Modeling of Nonlinear Stochastic Governing Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: HyperSINDy combines a variational encoder, hypernetwork, and trainable sparse binary mask to generate distributions over nonlinear governing equations and quantify uncertainty in higher-dimensional systems. It offers a deep generative alternative to PyDaDDy's pointwise Ito jump-moment regression, although its stochasticity is expressed through noise-driven coefficient generation rather than direct local estimation of a state-dependent diffusion tensor.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse recovery of Diffusion Dynamics: Handling High-Dimensionality in Repeated Short Trajectories
competitive_landscape.difference: Bayraktar and Dion-Blanc use a Lasso-regularized likelihood to estimate sparse high-dimensional drift from many independent short high-frequency diffusion trajectories, prove dimension- and trajectory-dependent convergence rates, and demonstrate variable selection on climate data. It directly addresses PyDaDDy's dimensionality and repeated-trajectory setting, but is adjacent rather than fully direct because it does not jointly discover a state-dependent diffusion function.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors present a unified, general, efficient, and user-friendly method that discovers interpretable stochastic dynamical equations directly from one- or two-dimensional time series, distinguishes noise-induced from deterministic states, provides diagnostics for validity, and is implemented in the open-source PyDaDDy package.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact 45-page arXiv v6 PDF combines finite-increment Kramers-Moyal targets with STLSQ, demonstrates four favorable scalar systems and six classic models, and reanalyzes published fish and cell datasets with residual, simulation, self-consistency, and left-out-summary checks. The package and immutable v1.1.1 archive are real and unusually accessible. However, stochastic SINDy, Stochastic Force Inference, and Langevin regression predate it; the fish and cell mechanisms were already reported; real-data validation is limited to histograms and autocorrelations; the cell residual violates Gaussianity; and the manuscript equations and archived multidimensional diagnostic code contain material inconsistencies.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest contribution is research infrastructure: an approachable biological SDE-discovery workflow with visualization, manual and automatic sparse fitting, example datasets, and multiple diagnostic prompts. Claims of methodological novelty, generally accurate equation discovery, or diagnostics that verify SDE assumptions should be narrowed. In particular, the exact numerical real-data results should not be promoted as fully verified until the printed residual formulas and archived F2, cross-diffusion, normalization, positivity, and hidden preprocessing issues are corrected and the analyses rerun with trajectory-level validation.

reviewer_notes: Read all 45 indexed pages of the exact cached arXiv v6 PDF, including 32 main-text pages, all equations, Table 1, Figures 1-6, complete discussion and references, plus the full 13-page supplement with Tables S1-S3 and Figures S1-S12. Every rendered page and visual was inspected. PDF and extracted-text hashes match the full-text index; all 45 pages contain usable text. The PDF title says 'ecological time series data' while the official arXiv v6 landing metadata says 'biological time series data'; both identify v6 revised 2024-09-22, and the journal version is American Naturalist 205 (2025), E100-E117, DOI 10.1086/734083. The linked immutable artifact was audited from Zenodo record 13777396, version v1.1.1_amnat_1, 25,101,128 bytes, MD5 1b52e4ec8f155b170559f848e4024345, snapshot directory 0db76ee. It contains GPL-3 source, six datasets, nine notebooks, documentation, and four simulation tests but no CI or locked environment. Source inspection confirmed the F1/F2 diffusion bug, cross-diffusion scaling bug, omitted diffusion normalization in generic analysis.py residual diagnostics, absolute-value simulation behavior, manual thresholds, and undisclosed mirror augmentation of cell trajectories; cell notebook 8 instead manually divides its derivative residual by sqrt(G22), matching the printed Equation 7 path after nondimensionalizing its sampling step to one. Artifact timebases remain internally inconsistent without an authoritative reconciliation: the paper and archived loader use fish 0.12 s and cell 1/6 h=10 min, while the archived README says 0.04 s and 15 min. Current GitHub master was checked at 44c84f3a93c7b86397ea3a6e905bdf9bcf3e2d6a (2026-06-10) and retains those code paths while still declaring 1.1.1; PyPI currently lists 1.0.0 and 0.1.5. Test collection in the audit environment stopped on the missing declared dependency plotly, so no scientific reproduction is claimed. Current official primary competitors and exact source versions, including HyperSINDy v1 and the UAI 2026 PMLR sparse-drift paper, were checked through 2026-08-24.
